newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain CiU hopes peseta to enter EMU at 85 per mark.
newsitem.headline: Spain CiU hopes peseta to enter EMU at 85 per mark.

text.p: Catalonia's Convergencia i Unio (CiU), the Spanish government's regional ally, said on Thursday it would prefer the peseta to enter monetary union at its current parity of 85.0718 versus the mark.
"It's a bit too early,...but to us the current parity seems a good point of reference," Francesc Homs, CiU's economic spokesman told Reuters in a interview.
"Other countries are more interested in using an average of the currencies' value in a given time. We are more interested in taking the central parity as a reference," he said.
On Thursday the peseta was trading at 84.19/20 per mark after dealers spoke of Bank of Spain mark purchases earlier in the morning when the mark hit a low at 84.13.
Homs added the outlook would be clearer after all countries have approved their respective 1998 budget.
"In October or November the list of countries entering the first wave (of European monetary union) will be clear. So it will be possible to define the differential in exchange rates," he said.
Despite the possibility of speculative attacks from the financial markets, he said political pressures will play a greater role as the start of Europe's single currency approaches.
"It's possible political power will surprise markets," he said.
He said the Catalan region, one of the richest in Spain, really backs entry into EMU.
"EMU has to be done," he said, adding that if, in an extreme case, it were delayed one year that should not change the outlook too much.
Regarding Spain's official money rate he said there is still scope for further reduction of by 1.0 to 1.25 percentage points from the present 5.25 percent rate.
"Between three percent in Germany and 5.25 percent in Spain there is a clear midvalue, around 3.5 or 4.0 percent which is where it is likely our official rate will be when the EMU starts," he said.
The ruling minority Popular Party (PP) government needs the CiU's legislative votes to pass its upcoming 1998 budget. The CiU backs the PP in an alliance but is not part of the government.
